headline: How One Farmer Is Proving Forest Protection Pays
meta_description: Cocoa farmer Susana Afrifa Ankrah shows how protecting Ghana's forests while growing sustainable crops can boost livelihoods by 80%.
summary_short: A Ghanaian cocoa farmer is demonstrating that conserving forests and earning better incomes aren't competing goals—they can thrive together.
body:
In the Atewa Range of south-eastern Ghana, cocoa farmer Susana Afrifa Ankrah is proving that protecting forests and improving livelihoods go hand-in-hand. Through the Ghana Cocoa Forest REDD+ Programme, launched in 2019, she has adopted farming methods that conserve trees and soil while boosting her income by approximately 80 percent. By planting native trees like African mahogany alongside her cocoa crops and using organic fertilisers and composting techniques, she now grows more beans from the same land while helping preserve the forest that shelters rare wildlife—from giant swallowtail butterflies to eagle owls and colobus monkeys. The programme, jointly run by Ghana's Forestry Commission and Cocoa Board, trains local farmers in shade-grown cocoa cultivation, which thrives under a tree canopy and actually produces yields as good as or better than conventional methods.

When the programme's representatives arrived in her community, Susana jumped at the opportunity. "I thought: 'This is a good initiative for me. I will not waste my time – I will get involved.'" The support extended beyond farming techniques—the programme provided practical equipment and business advice that helped her establish additional income streams. With guidance from the scheme, she set up a daycare nursery and bakery, now employing 17 workers. She has also diversified into beekeeping, raising pigs and snails, and growing vegetables including peppers, pawpaw, and cassava.

The initiative reflects a growing recognition that local communities, who have stewarded their land for generations, are essential to conservation. As Susana emphasises, the forest provides fresh air, cooling, rainfall, and medicinal remedies. By making her a partner in protection rather than asking her to choose between survival and conservation, the programme has created genuine incentive for forest preservation—proof that climate action and human dignity can flourish together.
